title: PepLLM: ESM-Guided Llama for Structured Protein-Peptide Binding Interface Analysis
summary: Protein-peptide interactions are central to cellular regulation and peptide-based drug discovery, yet existing computational methods mainly focus on interaction classification, binding-site prediction, or peptide binder generation. These formulations provide limited insight into the physicochemical mechanisms that determine how a peptide binds to a protein. In this work, we introduce \textbf{PepLLM}, an instruction-tuned framework for structured protein-peptide interface understanding. Given protein-peptide sequences, PepLLM generates a machine-readable JSON annotation describing multiple interface properties, including peptide burial state, hydrogen-bond density, salt-bridge presence, hotspot residues, hydrophobicity, and electrostatic complementarity. To support this task, we construct a new protein-peptide interface dataset by integrating structural interface analysis, solvent-accessible surface area computation, hydrophobic burial estimation, electrostatic potential calculation, and redundancy-aware data splitting. PepLLM connects a pretrained ESM encoder with a LLaMA decoder through a nonlinear modality adapter. The adapted ESM residue embeddings are injected into the LLaMA prompt as continuous soft tokens via placeholder-token replacement, enabling the decoder to generate structured interface annotations under instruction tuning. By moving beyond single-label prediction toward multi-property and mechanism-aware generation, PepLLM establishes a new task and modeling paradigm for interpretable protein-peptide interface analysis.

AI.tldr: PepLLM is an instruction-tuned LLM framework that generates structured JSON annotations describing multiple physicochemical properties of protein-peptide interfaces, using a protein encoder (ESM) connected to a text decoder (LLaMA) via a modality adapter.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for protein-peptide interactions are limited to classification, binding-site prediction, or binder generation, which provide little insight into the physicochemical mechanisms underlying peptide binding.
AI.method: PepLLM connects a pretrained ESM encoder with a LLaMA decoder through a nonlinear modality adapter. ESM residue embeddings are injected into the LLaMA prompt as continuous soft tokens via placeholder-token replacement, enabling structured interface annotation generation through instruction tuning. A new protein-peptide interface dataset is constructed via structural analysis, SASA computation, hydrophobic burial estimation, electrostatic potential calculation, and redundancy-aware data splitting.
AI.result: PepLLM generates machine-readable JSON annotations describing multiple interface properties including peptide burial state, hydrogen-bond density, salt-bridge presence, hotspot residues, hydrophobicity, and electrostatic complementarity.
AI.conclusion: PepLLM establishes a new task and modeling paradigm for interpretable, multi-property, and mechanism-aware protein-peptide interface analysis, moving beyond single-label prediction.

title: A Tensor Network Framework for Interpretable Graph Analysis of Brain Networks
summary: Identifying robust neurobiological signatures of brain disorders requires machine learning approaches that combine predictive performance with interpretable representations of feature interactions. Here we introduce a quantum-inspired framework based on tensor network machine learning that learns distributed representations of gray-matter features encoded in a Matrix Product State representation, a variational ansatz originally developed for quantum many-body systems. The trained model is then used not only as a classifier but to extract quantum connected correlations between features, which encode higher-order feature interactions and which we map onto a weighted graph. This construction allows us to track, within a single representation, both: (i) the global spectral properties of the network (capturing collective learning dynamics), and (ii) node-level centrality measures (providing interpretable signatures of individual brain regions). Using repeated train-test sampling schemes, we analyze two classification tasks on structural MRI data as examples of complex brain disorders: healthy controls versus schizophrenia and versus bipolar disorder. Node-level analysis identifies a stable set of gray-matter features, most prominently Heschl gyrus, insular cortex, and frontal regions, that act as hubs across multiple centrality measures and across resamplings. These centralities display lower variability across resamplings than Shapley values, supporting the interpretive value of the network representation. The bipolar feature set emerges as a subset of the schizophrenia one, consistent with the hierarchically organized neuroanatomical alterations reported in neuroimaging studies and offering a network-based characterization of this hierarchy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a quantum-inspired tensor network machine learning framework (Matrix Product State representation) for classifying brain disorders from structural MRI data. The approach learns distributed representations of gray-matter features, extracts quantum connected correlations mapped to weighted graphs, and provides both global spectral and node-level centrality analyses. Applied to schizophrenia vs. controls and bipolar disorder vs. controls, the method identifies stable hub regions (Heschl gyrus, insular cortex, frontal regions) with centralities that are more stable than Shapley values. Notably, the bipolar feature set is a subset of the schizophrenia set, consistent with hierarchical neuroanatomical alterations.
AI.motivation: To identify robust neurobiological signatures of brain disorders, there is a need for machine learning approaches that combine strong predictive performance with interpretable representations of feature interactions—something conventional classifiers often fail to provide.
AI.method: A quantum-inspired framework using tensor network machine learning with a Matrix Product State (MPS) representation encodes gray-matter features. The trained model serves both as a classifier and as a source of quantum connected correlations between features, which are mapped onto a weighted graph. Analysis tracks both global spectral properties (collective learning dynamics) and node-level centrality measures (interpretable brain region signatures) using repeated train-test sampling.
AI.result: On two classification tasks (healthy controls vs. schizophrenia and vs. bipolar disorder), node-level analysis identifies stable gray-matter hubs (Heschl gyrus, insular cortex, frontal regions) across centrality measures and resamplings. Centralities show lower variability than Shapley values across resamplings. The bipolar feature set is a subset of the schizophrenia set, consistent with hierarchical neuroanatomical alterations.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-inspired tensor network framework provides an interpretable, network-based characterization of brain disorders, offering stable hub identification and a hierarchical relationship between bipolar disorder and schizophrenia neuroanatomical signatures.

title: Scalable Enumeration of Pareto-optimal Polymers for Computing Equilibrium Concentrations
comment: Extended version of paper accepted at DNA 32: 32nd International Conference on DNA Computing and Molecular Programming. Includes appendix
summary: Predicting equilibrium concentrations of molecular complexes is essential for verifying the behavior of engineered DNA systems. However, a finite set of monomer types can in principle generate infinitely many complexes. We study this candidate-enumeration problem in a geometry-free, domain-level abstraction called a domain-monomer system, generalizing Thermodynamic Binding Networks (TBNs) to the unsaturated setting where not every possible bond need be formed. We define Pareto-suboptimal polymers as those that can be split into non-interacting parts, and show that restricting attention to Pareto-optimal polymers is thermodynamically justified: no Pareto-suboptimal polymer appears in any minimum free-energy configuration, and the total equilibrium concentration of such polymers is small. We prove that there are finitely many Pareto-optimal polymers and exactly characterize them via a Hilbert basis computation, extending prior work from the saturated TBN model. To scale this approach to large systems, we develop a framework that restricts the number of different monomer types that a single polymer contains, and uses combinatorial covering designs to reduce the number of Hilbert basis computations required. We benchmark the method on several families of DNA molecular programming systems, demonstrating order-of-magnitude speedups over direct computation while recovering nearly all equilibrium-relevant polymers.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the candidate-enumeration problem in domain-monomer systems (a generalization of Thermodynamic Binding Networks to unsaturated settings) for predicting equilibrium concentrations of molecular complexes. The authors define Pareto-suboptimal polymers (those splittable into non-interacting parts), prove that restricting to Pareto-optimal polymers is thermodynamically justified, characterize them exactly via Hilbert basis computation, and develop a scalable framework using combinatorial covering designs to reduce computation costs, achieving order-of-magnitude speedups on DNA molecular programming systems.
AI.motivation: Predicting equilibrium concentrations of molecular complexes is essential for verifying engineered DNA systems, but a finite set of monomer types can generate infinitely many complexes. This creates a fundamental enumeration challenge that must be solved to make equilibrium prediction tractable.
AI.method: The method generalizes Thermodynamic Binding Networks (TBNs) to unsaturated settings via domain-monomer systems. It introduces Pareto-optimal polymers (those that cannot be split into non-interacting parts), proves their thermodynamic justification, characterizes them exactly via Hilbert basis computation, and builds a scalable framework that restricts the number of monomer types per polymer and uses combinatorial covering designs to reduce the number of required Hilbert basis computations.
AI.result: The method is benchmarked on several families of DNA molecular programming systems, demonstrating order-of-magnitude speedups over direct computation while recovering nearly all equilibrium-relevant polymers.
AI.conclusion: Restricting equilibrium analysis to Pareto-optimal polymers is thermodynamically sound (no Pareto-suboptimal polymer appears in minimum free-energy configurations), finitely many such polymers exist and can be exactly characterized via Hilbert bases, and the proposed covering-design-based framework scales this approach to large systems with significant computational speedups.

title: Synthetic Wastewater Epidemiology Data Generation using Patterns-of-Life Simulation
summary: Wastewater contains rich biological signals that can be used to monitor population health, track infectious diseases, and detect emerging outbreaks. Pathogens and other biomarkers in sewage provide a unique, noninvasive view of disease prevalence at the community level. However, extracting these signals requires extensive field sampling, laboratory analysis, and expert interpretation. Consequently, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) datasets are scarce, geographically fragmented, and rarely released as open data. Even when available, existing datasets typically cover short time periods and limited geographic regions, restricting their usefulness for method development, benchmarking, and large-scale modeling. To address this gap, we present an application of an existing patterns-of-life simulation framework for generating synthetic infectious disease and wastewater pathogen datasets for wastewater-based epidemiology. Our approach extends a patterns-of-life simulation framework by using it as a model of human mobility and behavior while incorporating disease transmission and pathogen shedding dynamics. The resulting framework generates high-resolution spatial and temporal datasets capturing infection dynamics, mobility behavior, and wastewater-associated pathogen signals. We release a fully simulated dataset containing check-in records, social network links, infection states, pathogen loads, and ground-truth disease transmission information. These data support controlled experimentation for outbreak detection, source localization, resource allocation, surveillance strategy design, mobility-aware wastewater analysis, and targeted public health interventions. We provide datasets for Fulton County and demonstrate that the framework generalizes to other regions by generating data for any city with available OpenStreetMap information.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a synthetic data generation framework for wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE), extending a patterns-of-life simulation to model human mobility, disease transmission, and pathogen shedding. The framework produces high-resolution spatiotemporal datasets (check-ins, social networks, infection states, pathogen loads) for Fulton County and generalizes to any city with OpenStreetMap data, enabling controlled experimentation for outbreak detection and public health interventions.
AI.motivation: WBE datasets are scarce, geographically fragmented, rarely open, and typically cover short time periods and limited regions—restricting method development, benchmarking, and large-scale modeling. There is a need for comprehensive synthetic datasets to overcome these data limitations.
AI.method: Extends an existing patterns-of-life simulation framework by integrating disease transmission and pathogen shedding dynamics into the human mobility/behavior model, generating high-resolution synthetic spatial and temporal datasets with check-in records, social networks, infection states, pathogen loads, and ground-truth transmission data.
AI.result: A fully simulated dataset for Fulton County is released, and the framework is demonstrated to generalize to other regions by generating data for any city with available OpenStreetMap information.
AI.conclusion: The synthetic WBE dataset supports controlled experimentation for outbreak detection, source localization, resource allocation, surveillance strategy design, mobility-aware wastewater analysis, and targeted public health interventions, addressing the scarcity of real-world WBE data.

title: DNA Methylation Profiling in Melanoma: From Lesion Classification to Therapeutic Stratification
summary: DNA methylation provides a stable record of cellular identity, capturing epigenetic programs that distinguish specialized cell states despite a shared genome. Because malignant transformation and tumour progression are accompanied by extensive epigenetic remodeling, we hypothesized that the methylome of melanocytic lesions contains biologically and clinically relevant information for both diagnosis and disease progression. In a cohort of 1,001 tissue samples prospectively collected across eight German university hospitals profiled using Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC arrays, we compared machine-learning models based on selected Cytosine phosphate Guanine (CpG) methylation sites with models incorporating biology-guided features, including epigenetic age acceleration, cell type composition and copy-number variation burden. In an external test set, the best diagnostic classifier was CpG-based and distinguished melanocytic nevi, noninvasive melanoma and invasive melanoma with a macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.878 to 0.952). Notably, across CpGs most strongly hyper- and hypomethylated between NV and IM, NIM showed an intermediate methylation profile, providing a molecular correlate of its diagnostic complexity. The best model for clinically relevant treatment group prediction, with AJCC stages grouped according to guideline-based management recommendations, relied on biology-guided features and achieved a macro-averaged mean absolute error of 0.627 (95% CI: 0.477 to 0.808). Together, these findings demonstrate that methylation-based models can capture both diagnostic identity and clinically relevant disease stratification, supporting DNA methylation as a promising biomarker for further validation and potential clinical translation.

AI.tldr: This study profiles 1,001 melanocytic tissue samples using DNA methylation arrays and develops machine-learning models that distinguish melanocytic nevi, noninvasive melanoma, and invasive melanoma (AUC 0.919), while showing that biology-guided features (epigenetic age, cell type composition, CNV burden) are superior for predicting clinically relevant treatment groups (MAE 0.627), demonstrating DNA methylation as a promising biomarker for melanoma diagnosis and staging.
AI.motivation: To determine whether DNA methylation patterns in melanocytic lesions, which undergo extensive epigenetic remodeling during malignant transformation, can provide both diagnostic information and clinically relevant disease progression stratification despite shared genomic sequences.
AI.method: Prospectively collected 1,001 tissue samples across eight German university hospitals, profiled using Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC arrays. Compared machine-learning models based on selected CpG sites against models using biology-guided features (epigenetic age acceleration, cell type composition, copy-number variation burden), validated on an external test set, and grouped AJCC stages according to guideline-based management recommendations.
AI.result: The best diagnostic classifier (CpG-based) distinguished nevi, noninvasive melanoma, and invasive melanoma with macro-averaged AUC of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.878-0.952). Noninvasive melanoma showed an intermediate methylation profile between nevi and invasive melanoma, correlating with its diagnostic complexity. The best treatment group prediction model, based on biology-guided features, achieved a macro-averaged mean absolute error of 0.627 (95% CI: 0.477-0.808).
AI.conclusion: Methylation-based models capture both diagnostic identity and clinically relevant disease stratification, supporting DNA methylation as a promising biomarker for further validation and potential clinical translation in melanoma management.

title: Explainable AI-based Decision Support for Nocturnal Hypoglycemia Prevention in Type 1 Diabetes
summary: Purpose: Nocturnal hypoglycemia (NH) remains a challenge for individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D), particularly those who are physically active or on multiple daily injections (MDI). We leveraged an explainable evidential neural network model that forecasts minimum overnight glucose to identify NH risk factors and generate recommendations for NH prevention. Methods: We analyzed the impact of glucose and physical activity (PA) factors on predicted NH probability using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Data were from 20 adults with T1D on MDI (10 females; mean age 39 years; HbA1c 7\%) who participated in a cross-over study (NCT05967260). Results: A total of 502 nights were analyzed. Bedtime glucose was the strongest predictor of NH. Other relevant factors included recent exposure to high or low glucose, glucose variability before bedtime, and timing of PA. Some associations appeared physiologically counterintuitive, possibly reflecting behavioral adjustments. Based on the identified risk factors and their SHAP values, we determined key decision points and developed recommendations that may help prevent NH, such as consuming a bedtime snack or discussing potential adjustments to insulin therapy with a healthcare provider. Conclusion: Identifying predictors of NH offers insights for managing NH risk in clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: This study uses an explainable evidential neural network to forecast minimum overnight glucose and identify nocturnal hypoglycemia (NH) risk factors in adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, using SHAP analysis across 502 nights. Bedtime glucose was the strongest predictor, with other factors including glucose variability, recent glucose exposure, and physical activity timing, leading to practical recommendations like bedtime snacks or insulin adjustments.
AI.motivation: Nocturnal hypoglycemia remains a significant challenge for individuals with type 1 diabetes, especially those who are physically active or on multiple daily injections. There is a need for interpretable predictive models that can identify NH risk factors and generate actionable recommendations for prevention.
AI.method: An explainable evidential neural network model was developed to forecast minimum overnight glucose. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to analyze the impact of glucose and physical activity factors on predicted NH probability. Data came from 20 adults with T1D on MDI in a cross-over study.
AI.result: Analysis of 502 nights revealed bedtime glucose as the strongest NH predictor. Other relevant factors included recent exposure to high or low glucose, glucose variability before bedtime, and physical activity timing. Some associations appeared physiologically counterintuitive, possibly reflecting behavioral adjustments. Key decision points and recommendations were developed, such as bedtime snacks or discussing insulin therapy adjustments with healthcare providers.
AI.conclusion: Identifying NH predictors through explainable AI offers valuable insights for managing nocturnal hypoglycemia risk and supports clinical decision-making for individuals with type 1 diabetes.

title: Motional Degrees of Freedom in Network Hamiltonian Models
summary: Network Hamiltonian Models (NHMs) provide an efficient framework for modeling the aggregation of interacting particles (e.g., the condensation of proteins into gel-like, oligomeric, or fibrillar states), representing the system as a network whose edges represent bound interactions. Terms within the network Hamiltonian represent multi-body interactions governing aggregation behavior, and are specified via topological degrees of freedom. Because motional degrees of freedom are not explicitly represented within the NHM, their influence must be indirectly accounted for by introduction of corresponding terms to the Hamiltonian. Here, we describe specifications for terms representing motional degrees of freedom of two, three, and four-body interactions. We also consider the impact of these terms on the aggregation states of a minimal system governed only by a pairwise edge potential, showing that three and four-body interactions favor condensation of the system into small droplet-like structures at low temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces specifications for Hamiltonian terms representing motional degrees of freedom in Network Hamiltonian Models (NHMs), covering two-, three-, and four-body interactions, and demonstrates that three and four-body terms promote condensation into small droplet-like structures at low temperature in a minimal pairwise system.
AI.motivation: Network Hamiltonian Models (NHMs) offer an efficient way to model aggregation of interacting particles, but motional degrees of freedom are not explicitly represented. Since these motions influence aggregation behavior indirectly, there is a need to define specific Hamiltonian terms that account for their effects across different multi-body interaction orders.
AI.method: The authors define specifications for Hamiltonian terms that represent motional degrees of freedom for two-, three-, and four-body interactions within the NHM framework. They then analyze a minimal system governed only by a pairwise edge potential to test the impact of these new terms on aggregation states.
AI.result: The analysis shows that introducing three- and four-body interaction terms favors condensation of the system into small droplet-like structures at low temperature, whereas the minimal pairwise-only system behaves differently without these terms.
AI.conclusion: Motional degrees of freedom can be effectively encoded in NHMs via multi-body Hamiltonian terms, and these terms significantly alter aggregation behavior—specifically promoting droplet formation at low temperature—highlighting their importance for accurate aggregation modeling.

title: A Conditional Structure-Aware Generative Transformer for Multi-Objective Design of m1Ψ-Modified RNA 5' UTRs
summary: The 5' untranslated region is a major determinant of translation initiation, and its effect becomes especially important in modified mRNA sequences, where start-codon context, cap-proximal secondary structure, upstream AUGs and upstream open reading frames, and nucleotide chemistry can alter ribosome scanning and initiation recruitment, scanning, and decoding in sequence-dependent ways. Recent computational studies have moved the field from prediction toward design, including massively trained predictive models such as Smart5UTR for m1$Ψ$-modified mRNA, broader 5' UTR generation and optimization frameworks such as UTRGAN and UTailoR, and structure-guided RNA design systems such as RhoDesign. Here, we describe a conditional generative framework for 50-nt modified-RNA 5' UTR design that optionally conditions on ribosome load, GC content, minimum free energy, and target secondary structure. The implementation uses a Transformer-based generator followed by sequence ranking and local refinement with a Smart5UTR-derived ribosome-load oracle and ViennaRNA-based folding metrics, including support for modified-base folding parameters. Across multiple simulation scenarios and experimental settings, different combinations of RL, GC, MFE, and structural constraints produced distinct performance tradeoffs, enabling ablation-based identification of the best-performing formulation.

AI.tldr: A conditional generative framework for designing 50-nucleotide modified-RNA 5' UTRs, optionally conditioning on ribosome load, GC content, minimum free energy, and target secondary structure, using a Transformer-based generator with Smart5UTR-derived ribosome-load oracle and ViennaRNA-based folding metrics.
AI.motivation: The 5' untranslated region (UTR) is a major determinant of translation initiation, especially in modified mRNA sequences where multiple factors (start-codon context, secondary structure, upstream AUGs/uORFs, nucleotide chemistry) affect ribosome scanning in sequence-dependent ways. While prior work has moved from prediction to design, a framework is needed that can conditionally generate 5' UTRs with controllable biophysical and functional properties.
AI.method: A conditional generative framework for 50-nt modified-RNA 5' UTR design that optionally conditions on ribosome load (RL), GC content, minimum free energy (MFE), and target secondary structure. It uses a Transformer-based generator followed by sequence ranking and local refinement with a Smart5UTR-derived ribosome-load oracle and ViennaRNA-based folding metrics, including support for modified-base folding parameters.
AI.result: Across multiple simulation scenarios and experimental settings, different combinations of RL, GC, MFE, and structural constraints produced distinct performance tradeoffs, enabling ablation-based identification of the best-performing formulation.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables controllable, conditionable design of modified-RNA 5' UTRs with tunable tradeoffs across ribosome load and biophysical constraints, with ablation analysis revealing the optimal constraint formulation.

title: Forward and reverse delay-driven hippocampal replay without symmetric plasticity
summary: Hippocampal replay is a phenomenon observed in mammals and songbirds where neural activation sequences experienced during wakeful periods are repeated during rest or sleep. This mechanism is believed to play a crucial role in episodic memory consolidation, retrieval, and planning. Interestingly, replay can occur in both forward and reverse temporal orders and across a wide range of increased speeds. The learning of activation sequences has traditionally been modeled by temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity rules, which explain replay as a chain of activity. The inability of such rules to strengthen backward connections has led to the widespread belief that they cannot account for bidirectional replay. Existing theoretical work therefore explains reverse replay through symmetric connections, which would be formed through symmetric plasticity rules. We propose a delay-coupled neural field model of CA3, where activity propagates as a wave in a ring, and replays occur both forwards and backwards at different speeds. Our model can learn bidirectional replay after a single noisy exposure to a stimulus with either symmetric or asymmetric plasticity. We derive a low-dimensional description of the dynamics and analyze the stability of possible replay speeds.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a delay-coupled neural field model of CA3 that explains bidirectional hippocampal replay (forward and reverse) after a single noisy stimulus exposure, using either symmetric or asymmetric plasticity rules—challenging the common belief that asymmetric Hebbian rules cannot produce reverse replay.
AI.motivation: Traditional temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity models can explain forward replay as activity chains but cannot strengthen backward connections, leading to the widespread belief that reverse replay requires symmetric plasticity. The authors aim to resolve this theoretical gap by showing bidirectional replay can emerge from a single framework.
AI.method: The authors develop a delay-coupled neural field model of CA3 where activity propagates as a wave on a ring. They demonstrate that bidirectional replay can be learned after a single noisy stimulus exposure with either symmetric or asymmetric plasticity, and derive a low-dimensional dynamical description to analyze the stability of possible replay speeds.
AI.result: The model successfully produces both forward and backward replay at different speeds within a unified framework, showing that asymmetric plasticity is not inherently incapable of supporting reverse replay as previously assumed.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional hippocampal replay can be accounted for by a delay-coupled neural field model using symmetric or asymmetric plasticity, providing a more flexible theoretical basis for understanding replay phenomena in memory consolidation.

title: Phenotypic Assortment and the Evolution of Cooperation in Finite Periodic Phenotype Spaces
summary: We study the evolution of cooperation in a finite haploid population whose individuals carry both a strategy and a phenotype on a finite periodic space. Cooperators help with a probability that decays exponentially with phenotypic distance, generating graded phenotype-dependent assortment. Under weak selection and a large-population mutation scaling, we combine coalescent arguments with the spectral representation of a random walk on the discrete torus to derive an explicit benefit-to-cost threshold for cooperation to be favored in stationary abundance. Stronger phenotypic discrimination and higher phenotype-space dimension strictly lower this threshold, whereas strategy mutation raises it. In contrast, phenotype mutation has a nonmonotone effect: the threshold diverges for both very rare and very rapid phenotype mutation and therefore attains at least one minimum at an intermediate rate. The high-mutation inhibition results from mixing on the finite phenotype space and distinguishes the periodic model from its unbounded-lattice counterpart.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a mathematical population-genetic model showing how graded phenotype-dependent assortment (via exponentially decaying cooperation probability with phenotypic distance) shapes the evolution of cooperation on a finite periodic space. Using coalescent theory and spectral analysis of random walks on discrete tori, the authors derive an explicit benefit-to-cost threshold for cooperation favored under weak selection. They find that stronger discrimination and higher phenotype-space dimension lower the threshold, strategy mutation raises it, and phenotype mutation shows a nonmonotone effect with a minimum at intermediate rates due to finite-space mixing.
AI.motivation: To understand how phenotypic structure and graded assortment influence the evolution of cooperation, going beyond binary or unbounded phenotype models to investigate finite periodic phenotype spaces with realistic distance-dependent cooperative behavior.
AI.method: The authors model a finite haploid population on a finite periodic space, where cooperation probability decays exponentially with phenotypic distance. They combine coalescent theory with spectral representation of a random walk on the discrete torus under weak selection and large-population mutation scaling to derive an explicit benefit-to-cost threshold.
AI.result: Stronger phenotypic discrimination and higher phenotype-space dimension strictly lower the benefit-to-cost threshold for cooperation. Strategy mutation raises the threshold. Phenotype mutation has a nonmonotone effect: the threshold diverges for both very rare and very rapid phenotype mutation, achieving at least one minimum at intermediate rates. High-mutation inhibition arises from finite phenotype space mixing, distinguishing this model from the unbounded-lattice case.
AI.conclusion: The periodic finite phenotype space introduces qualitatively distinct dynamics compared to unbounded lattices, particularly the nonmonotone effect of phenotype mutation, highlighting the importance of finite phenotype space geometry in the evolution of cooperation.

title: DigiPhen: a new paradigm for building predictive models of biological systems
summary: Reengineered biological systems have the potential to revolutionize chemical and material production, enhance critical mineral recovery, serve as threat sensors and improve human health. Unfortunately, the extreme complexity of organisms has made it difficult to achieve this potential in all but the simplest cases. Recent technological advances, however, have provided a foundation for solving this problem. Here, we describe a capability for accelerating the reengineering of cells by providing accurate predictions of the impact of genetic or environmental changes on cell phenotype. This digital phenome platform (DigiPhen) consists of integrated experimental, analytical and modeling workflows for building a digital representation of microbial or plant systems. It is designed around an expanding set of interchangeable, interconnecting software and experimental modules that can accurately represent the mechanistic determinants of phenotype. The DigiPhen platform will systematically collect data on cell composition, spatial organization, metabolic pathways and regulatory networks in a semi-autonomous fashion and use this information to build modular, multi-scale models of biological systems. These models will be used to predict molecular and environmental changes needed for producing desired biological outcomes. DigiPhen is intended to be the heart of community research campaigns that will meet the immediate needs of individual researchers while fulfilling long-term goals of the scientific community. Altogether, the DigiPhen platform represents a new paradigm for building predictive models of biological systems.

AI.tldr: This paper describes DigiPhen, an integrated platform combining experimental, analytical, and modeling workflows to build digital representations (digital phenomes) of microbial or plant systems. It aims to provide accurate predictions of how genetic or environmental changes impact cell phenotype by systematically collecting data on cell composition, spatial organization, metabolic pathways, and regulatory networks to construct modular, multi-scale mechanistic models.
AI.motivation: Biological systems have the potential to revolutionize chemical production, mineral recovery, threat sensing, and human health, but the extreme complexity of organisms has made it difficult to achieve this potential except in the simplest cases. There is a need for a capability to accelerate cell reengineering through accurate phenotype prediction.
AI.method: DigiPhen integrates experimental, analytical, and modeling workflows to build digital representations of biological systems. It consists of interchangeable, interconnecting software and experimental modules that represent mechanistic determinants of phenotype. The platform semi-autonomously collects data on cell composition, spatial organization, metabolic pathways, and regulatory networks to build modular, multi-scale models of biological systems.
AI.result: The paper describes the DigiPhen platform concept rather than presenting experimental results. It establishes the architecture and design principles for building predictive models of biological systems, intended to serve as the centerpiece of community research campaigns addressing both immediate researcher needs and long-term scientific community goals.
AI.conclusion: DigiPhen represents a new paradigm for building predictive models of biological systems, providing a foundation for accelerating the reengineering of cells by accurately predicting the impact of genetic or environmental changes on cell phenotype.

title: The first major transition: Origin of life from a multilevel selection perspective
summary: The origin of life is the first, arguably, the most important and also the most enigmatic major transition in evolution (MTE). As all MTE, the transition at the origin of life can be constructively addressed only within the conceptual framework of multilevel selection. The two levels of selection relevant for the origin of life are replicators, and reproducers, that is, compartments (protocells) capable of reproduction via a primitive form of division. The symbiotic model for the origin of life presented here posits that cellular life was preceded by protocells that harbored proto-metabolic networks but not genetic elements (replicators), Replicators could have started as selfish elements inside protocells selected only for replication efficiency, but subsequently, would evolve into mutualists such that the reproducer-replicator union became a new, collective unit of selection. Mathematical modeling of replicator-reproducer coevolution identifies the conditions under which replicator-carrying protocells can outcompete empty protocells. For the replicator-carrying protocells to and get fixed in evolution, replication has to be coupled with protocell division, selection for the highest replication rate being partially suppressed. At the earliest stages of evolution, random, stochastic protocell division was advantageous compared to symmetrical division. The multilevel selection perspective illuminates the likely order of key events on the evolutionary route from ensembles of chemicals to cells endowed with genomes, symmetrical cell division and anti-parasite defense systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a symbiotic model for the origin of life within a multilevel selection framework, positing that protocells (reproducers) harbored proto-metabolic networks before acquiring genetic replicators, which initially existed as selfish elements before evolving into mutualists. Mathematical modeling shows that replicator-carrying protocells can outcompete empty ones when replication is coupled with protocell division and replication rate selection is partially suppressed, with stochastic division being advantageous at the earliest stages.
AI.motivation: The origin of life is considered the first, most important, and most enigmatic major transition in evolution (MTE). The authors argue that this transition can only be constructively addressed through the conceptual framework of multilevel selection, which has been lacking in previous approaches to understanding life's origins.
AI.method: The paper uses a conceptual multilevel selection framework combined with mathematical modeling of replicator-reproducer coevolution to identify conditions under which replicator-carrying protocells can outcompete empty protocells and become fixed in evolution.
AI.result: The models identify that for replicator-carrying protocells to become fixed, replication must be coupled with protocell division, and selection for the highest replication rate must be partially suppressed. Furthermore, at the earliest stages, random stochastic protocell division was advantageous compared to symmetrical division.
AI.conclusion: The multilevel selection perspective illuminates the likely order of key events on the evolutionary route from ensembles of chemicals to cells endowed with genomes, symmetrical cell division, and anti-parasite defense systems, establishing a coherent evolutionary narrative for the origin of life.

title: Temporal filling-in reduces attentional fluctuations in sustained visual attention
summary: Our capacity to maintain focus on task-relevant goals over time is constrained because attentional states wax and wane moment to moment. One theoretical account posits that temporal filling-in - filling temporal blank intervals between target stimuli - reduces attentional fluctuations to enhance sustained attention. This proposal, however, lacks direct empirical validation given the difficulty of tracking attentional fluctuations via behavioral measurements. To resolve this gap, we combined a visual timing task that assessed the behavioral benefit of temporal filling-in with electroencephalographic recordings of visual steady-state evoked potentials (SSEPs), which tracked neural responses associated with periodic attentional fluctuations entrained to the rhythmic visual sequence. Behavioral improvements in sustained attention via temporal filling-in were associated with reduced attentional fluctuations, as indexed by attenuated visual SSEP amplitudes. The findings highlight a fundamental neural mechanism whereby temporal filling-in reduces attentional fluctuations to stabilize sustained visual attention over extended periods.

AI.tldr: This study combines a visual timing task with EEG recordings of steady-state evoked potentials (SSEPs) to provide the first direct empirical evidence that temporal filling-in (filling blank intervals between target stimuli) reduces attentional fluctuations and enhances sustained attention over time.
AI.motivation: While theoretical accounts propose that temporal filling-in reduces attentional fluctuations to enhance sustained attention, this proposal lacked direct empirical validation because tracking attentional fluctuations via behavioral measurements alone is difficult.
AI.method: The researchers combined a visual timing task (assessing the behavioral benefit of temporal filling-in) with electroencephalographic recordings of visual steady-state evoked potentials (SSEPs), which tracked neural responses associated with periodic attentional fluctuations entrained to the rhythmic visual sequence.
AI.result: Behavioral improvements in sustained attention via temporal filling-in were associated with reduced attentional fluctuations, as indexed by attenuated visual SSEP amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a fundamental neural mechanism whereby temporal filling-in reduces attentional fluctuations to stabilize sustained visual attention over extended periods.

title: Uncovering Cellular Resolution in scRNAseq via Unbiased Cell and Gene Network Analysis
summary: Conventional annotation of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data relies heavily on manual, marker-based thresholding, an approach that can obscure subtle transcriptomic gradients and collapse functionally distinct cell states into broad, heterogeneous populations. Here we apply the Gaussian multi-Graphical Model (GmGM) framework, which jointly infers cell-cell and gene-gene dependency structure from a single scRNA-seq data matrix, to a 10x Genomics PBMC dataset. Ten independent GMGM-Leiden clustering runs were integrated into a robust consensus partition using a soft cluster ensemble approach and benchmarked against reference cell-type annotations. This strategy yielded stable cluster partitions that resolve biologically meaningful sub-populations not distinguished by the reference annotation. In parallel, for each cluster, gene co-expression modules were extracted from the fitted model via consensus Leiden clustering across resolutions, evaluated using standard network metrics, and validated functionally with the Network Enrichment Analysis Test (NEAT), which confirmed non-random enrichment signal. A module-scoring procedure linked network topology to per-cell, per-cluster expression signatures, and a novel extension of GmGM, recovering a shared cell-cell network together with population-specific gene networks in a single model run, was demonstrated in a case study on the CD4+ T-cell population. These results indicate that GmGM provides a unified, reproducible framework for joint cell clustering and gene-network inference, capable of revealing cellular structure beyond that captured by conventional pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper applies the Gaussian multi-Graphical Model (GmGM) to scRNA-seq data, jointly inferring cell-cell and gene-gene networks. Using consensus clustering (GMGM-Leiden) on a PBMC dataset, it identifies biologically meaningful sub-populations beyond conventional annotation, extracts validated gene co-expression modules, and introduces an extension recovering shared cell networks with population-specific gene networks.
AI.motivation: Conventional scRNA-seq annotation relies on manual, marker-based thresholding that can obscure subtle transcriptomic gradients and collapse distinct cell states into broad heterogeneous populations, motivating a need for unsupervised, graph-based frameworks that capture finer cellular structure.
AI.method: The GmGM framework jointly infers cell-cell and gene-gene dependency structures from scRNA-seq data. Ten GMGM-Leiden clustering runs are integrated via a soft cluster ensemble into a consensus partition. For each cluster, gene co-expression modules are extracted via consensus Leiden clustering across resolutions, evaluated with network metrics, and validated with NEAT. A module-scoring procedure links network topology to expression signatures, and a GmGM extension recovers shared cell-cell networks with population-specific gene networks.
AI.result: Consensus partitions were stable and resolved sub-populations not distinguished by reference annotations. Extracted gene modules showed non-random functional enrichment (validated by NEAT). The GmGM extension was demonstrated on the CD4+ T-cell population, recovering shared and population-specific networks.
AI.conclusion: GmGM provides a unified, reproducible framework for joint cell clustering and gene-network inference, capable of revealing cellular structure beyond conventional pipelines.

title: Systematic pathway comparison on the powerset of rule-based biochemical systems
summary: Computational pathway design often focuses on evaluating selected pathways or optimizing fluxes in a fixed network, but gives less direct access to the combinatorial question of which other enzyme subsets of the network can support productive alternative pathways. A structured computational analysis of these networks can act as a valuable pre-step to the pathway design process. We present here a systematic approach for exploring biochemical pathway alternatives across enzyme subsets, using a computational methodology based on a rule-based modeling of the enzymes: for a biochemical system with enzyme set $S$, we evaluate all subsets $s \subseteq S$ by generating chemical reaction spaces, searching for integer-hyperflow pathways from prescribed inputs to target products, and organizing feasible subsets by set inclusion. This yields an inclusion-ordered landscape of pathway feasibility and carbon efficiency. We apply the approach to the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, to non-oxidative glycolysis, and to glycolysis. Across these systems, feasible subsets occupy only a moderate fraction of all enzyme subsets, but the structure of this feasible region differs strongly between the systems. Larger enzyme sets do not consistently improve carbon efficiency when every enzyme in the tested subset is required to participate in the pathway. Instead, performance depends on specific enzyme combinations. The resulting subset landscapes are valuable means for identifying essential enzymes, candidate redundancies, and small high-performing enzyme subsets. By making the enzyme-subset landscape itself the object of analysis, the approach addresses the gap between detailed evaluation of individual candidate pathways and early-stage design decisions about which enzyme combinations are worth investigating at all.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic computational approach for exploring alternative biochemical pathways across all enzyme subsets of a network. Using rule-based enzyme modeling, the method generates chemical reaction spaces for each enzyme subset, searches for integer-hyperflow pathways from inputs to targets, and organizes feasible subsets by set inclusion to create an inclusion-ordered landscape of pathway feasibility and carbon efficiency. Applied to the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, non-oxidative glycolysis, and glycolysis, the approach reveals that only a moderate fraction of enzyme subsets are feasible, that larger enzyme sets do not consistently improve carbon efficiency, and that performance depends on specific enzyme combinations—making the subset landscape itself the object of analysis for identifying essential enzymes, redundancies, and high-performing enzyme subsets.
AI.motivation: Traditional computational pathway design focuses on evaluating selected pathways or optimizing fluxes within a fixed network, but fails to directly address the combinatorial question of which enzyme subsets can support productive alternative pathways. There is a gap between detailed evaluation of individual candidate pathways and early-stage design decisions about which enzyme combinations are worth investigating at all, which this work aims to fill.
AI.method: The approach builds on rule-based modeling of enzymes: for each enzyme subset s of the full enzyme set S, the method generates the corresponding chemical reaction space, searches for integer-hyperflow pathways from specified inputs to target products, and organizes the feasible subsets by set inclusion. This produces an inclusion-ordered landscape of pathway feasibility and carbon efficiency across all enzyme subsets.
AI.result: Applied to the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, non-oxidative glycolysis, and glycolysis, only a moderate fraction of enzyme subsets are feasible; the structure of the feasible region differs strongly between systems. Larger enzyme sets do not consistently improve carbon efficiency when all enzymes in a subset must participate; performance instead depends on specific enzyme combinations. The subset landscapes identify essential enzymes, candidate redundancies, and small high-performing enzyme subsets.
AI.conclusion: Making the enzyme-subset landscape itself the object of analysis bridges the gap between detailed evaluation of individual candidate pathways and early-stage design decisions. The method provides a valuable pre-step to pathway design by systematically mapping which enzyme combinations are feasible and high-performing before committing to detailed pathway analysis.

title: Dendritic structure enables powerful plasticity
summary: Over the past decades, it has become increasingly clear that the complex morphology of cortical neurons is more than just a quirk of evolution, and that dendritic compartments serve as computational elements in their own right, rather than just providing connections between nerve cell bodies. While most computational studies discuss the enhanced representational capabilities of multi-compartment models as compared to point neurons, we focus here on the implications of neuronal morphology for synaptic plasticity. We argue that the ability of single neurons to simultaneously encode multiple pieces of information gives synapses local access to more than just the classical Hebbian pre- and postsynaptic terms, and with much greater specificity and reaction speed than permitted by other globally modulated factors. Based on a comparative review of recent dendritic learning models, we show how such neuronal compartmentalization can provide synapses with the means for calculating various forms of error signals, which in turn give rise to powerful real-time and fully local instantiations of deep learning through gradient descent. Implemented within cortical microcircuits capable of propagating and manipulating these errors, compartmentalized neurons thus ultimately enable the learning of far more complex tasks than are achievable by globally modulated Hebbian plasticity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that the compartmentalized morphology of cortical neurons enables local, real-time forms of deep learning through gradient descent, by providing synapses access to error signals far richer than classical Hebbian learning allows.
AI.motivation: While multi-compartment neuron models are often discussed for their enhanced representational capabilities, their implications for synaptic plasticity remain underexplored. The authors seek to highlight how dendritic compartments provide synapses local, fast access to error signals that go beyond classical Hebbian terms and global modulation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comparative review of recent dendritic learning models, examining how neuronal compartmentalization enables synapses to compute various forms of error signals, and how these can be implemented within cortical microcircuits to propagate and manipulate errors for gradient-descent-based learning.
AI.result: Compartmentalized neurons can implement powerful real-time and fully local instantiations of deep learning through gradient descent, enabling the learning of far more complex tasks than achievable by globally modulated Hebbian plasticity alone.
AI.conclusion: The ability of single neurons to encode multiple pieces of information simultaneously gives synapses access to specific, fast error signals, and when embedded in cortical microcircuits, compartmentalized neurons support deep learning beyond the capabilities of global Hebbian plasticity.

title: Episode Clustering in Phylogenetic Networks
comment: Preprint version submitted to ECCB 2026 before peer review. A revised version has been accepted for publication in Bioinformatics as part of the ECCB 2026 Proceedings
summary: The classical duplication episode clustering (EC) model introduced by Guigó et al. in the 1990s provides a foundational approach for inferring genomic duplication events crucial to understanding genome evolution. This model clusters single gene duplications from a collection of gene trees at locations in the species tree to minimize the total number of such locations, called duplication episodes. Here, we introduce NetEC, a novel extension of this problem to phylogenetic networks. To solve NetEC, we first develop a polynomial-time dynamic programming (DP) algorithm for testing whether a given set of network nodes can serve as episode locations. We then propose a main inference algorithm that utilizes this DP component to optimize the episode count; while the feasibility test runs in polynomial time, the full optimization has exponential worst-case complexity, and an optional heuristic mode is provided for larger instances. We also propose an extended episode analysis procedure that identifies additional genomic duplication candidates below reticulation nodes, complementing the main algorithm by resolving potential upward clustering of duplications induced by reticulation. We evaluate our method on simulated data and on an empirical Pandanales dataset comprising over 29,000 gene trees, demonstrating exact and accurate inference of genomic duplication events even in the presence of multiple reticulations.

AI.tldr: NetEC extends the classical duplication episode clustering (EC) model to phylogenetic networks, providing algorithms for inferring genomic duplication events on networks with reticulations, and demonstrates exact and accurate inference on simulated and empirical data.
AI.motivation: The classical EC model clusters gene duplications on species trees but cannot handle phylogenetic networks, which are needed to represent reticulate evolutionary events (e.g., hybridization, introgression). A network-based extension is necessary for accurate genome evolution inference.
AI.method: NetEC introduces a polynomial-time dynamic programming (DP) algorithm for testing whether a given set of network nodes can serve as duplication episode locations, followed by a main inference algorithm using this DP for optimization (exponential worst-case, with optional heuristic mode). An extended episode analysis identifies duplication candidates below reticulation nodes.
AI.result: Evaluation on simulated data and an empirical Pandanales dataset with over 29,000 gene trees demonstrates exact and accurate inference of genomic duplication events even with multiple reticulations present.
AI.conclusion: NetEC successfully extends duplication episode clustering to phylogenetic networks, enabling accurate duplication event inference in complex evolutionary scenarios involving reticulation.

title: Beyond chlorophyll: machine learning estimates of diagnostic phytoplankton pigments from multispectral ocean colour data
comment: Submitted to Frontiers of Marine Science. 21 pages, 8 Figures
summary: Phytoplankton play a central role in marine ecosystems and the global carbon cycle, with different groups contributing differently to ocean biogeochemical processes. While standard techniques exist for monitoring phytoplankton concentration from ocean-colour data, their community composition remains difficult to observe at large scales. Chlorophyll-a, widely available from satellite ocean-colour observations, is commonly used as a measure of phytoplankton biomass but provides limited information on taxonomic composition. Accessory pigments, some of which are diagnostic of important phytoplankton groups, offer additional information on community structure, but their retrieval from ocean-colour data is challenging because of limited spectral resolution and strong covariance with chlorophyll-a. In this study, we evaluate machine learning methods for estimating diagnostic pigment concentrations from multispectral satellite observations. Using a global dataset of 33,640 High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) measurements matched with ESA Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative (OC-CCI) reflectance data, we compare Random Forest and TabPFN models trained on multispectral reflectance with baseline models using chlorophyll-a alone. A temporally stratified validation scheme is employed to reduce the effects of autocorrelation. Results show that multispectral models consistently outperform approaches based solely on satellite-derived chlorophyll-a, demonstrating that ocean-colour reflectance contains additional information relevant to pigment discrimination. Improvements vary by pigment, with those strongly correlated with chlorophyll-a showing limited gains, while others exhibit substantial improvement. These findings highlight the potential of machine learning to extract ecologically relevant information from satellite data beyond conventional chlorophyll-based approaches.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates machine learning methods (Random Forest and TabPFN) for estimating diagnostic pigment concentrations from multispectral satellite ocean-colour data, using 33,640 HPLC measurements matched with OC-CCI reflectance data. Multispectral models outperform chlorophyll-a-only baselines, though gains vary by pigment, demonstrating that ocean-colour reflectance contains additional information for pigment discrimination beyond chlorophyll-a.
AI.motivation: Phytoplankton community composition is difficult to observe at large scales from satellite data. While chlorophyll-a is widely available as a biomass proxy, it provides limited taxonomic information. Diagnostic accessory pigments could reveal community structure, but their retrieval from multispectral ocean-colour data is challenging due to limited spectral resolution and strong covariance with chlorophyll-a.
AI.method: Machine learning models (Random Forest and TabPFN) are trained on multispectral OC-CCI reflectance data to estimate diagnostic pigment concentrations. These are compared against baseline models using only satellite-derived chlorophyll-a. A global dataset of 33,640 HPLC measurements is used, with a temporally stratified validation scheme to reduce autocorrelation effects.
AI.result: Multispectral models consistently outperform chlorophyll-a-only baselines. Improvement varies by pigment: pigments strongly correlated with chlorophyll-a show limited gains, while others exhibit substantial improvement.
AI.conclusion: Ocean-colour reflectance contains additional information beyond chlorophyll-a that is relevant for pigment discrimination. Machine learning shows potential for extracting ecologically relevant phytoplankton community composition information from satellite data at large scales.

title: Analysis of correlations of dwell-times of adjacent kinetic states in the activity of the cold and menthol receptor TRPM8
summary: Temperature-sensitive transient receptor potential (TRP) channels play a significant role in intercellular signalling in response to membrane depolarisation and caclium influx. TRPM8 ion channels have been investigated as the main cold receptors (neurosensors), but they can also be activated by voltage, $Ca^{2+}$ store depletion, and certain lipids and other ligands that induce cold sensation (such as menthol and icilin). Despite recent progress in studying these channels at the single-channel level, the mechanisms and time course of their activation remain underexplored. We propose an approach to single-ion channel analysis that elucidates the presence of correlations between dwell-times of adjacent open and closed states. One of the major benefits of this approach is that it can serve as an express test of channel activity properties owing to its simplicity and fast numerical realization. The idea of our analysis is to study the difference between the distribution function derived from the given trace (simulated or experimentally recorded) and the predicted distributions of simple models without correlation. In this way, we compared the distribution function of the difference between the durations of the adjacent open and closed states of the channel, as well as that of a similar sequence of open-closed-open-closed states.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel approach to single-ion channel analysis that detects correlations between dwell-times of adjacent open and closed states, serving as a fast express test of channel activity properties, particularly applied to TRPM8 ion channels.
AI.motivation: TRPM8 ion channels are key cold receptors but their activation mechanisms and time course remain underexplored despite recent progress in single-channel studies. There is a need for a simple and fast method to characterize channel activity beyond basic single-channel analysis.
AI.method: The method compares the distribution function derived from a given trace (simulated or experimental) with predicted distributions from simple models without correlation. They study the difference between durations of adjacent open and closed states, as well as similar open-closed-open-closed state sequences, to detection correlations between adjacent dwell-times.
AI.result: The approach successfully elucidates correlations between dwell-times of adjacent open and closed states, offering a fast and simple numerical realization as an express test of channel activity properties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed single-ion channel analysis approach provides a practical and efficient tool for probing TRPM8 channel activation dynamics, complementing existing single-channel studies with a rapid correlation-detection method.

title: PHASE: encoding global protein ensembles with local Hamiltonians and all-atom backmapping
summary: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, which can be viewed as high-dimensional probability distributions over molecular conformations. Yet the statistical organization of these distributions is often represented only implicitly, either through collections of simulation trajectories or within high-capacity generative models. Here, we introduce PHASE (Protein Hamiltonians for Sampling of Ensembles), a system-specific framework that converts atomistic conformational ensembles into an explicit and interpretable statistical model. Applied to ten conformational ensembles derived from approximately 37$μ$s of atomistic simulations of the adenosine A2A receptor, Hamiltonians containing only local residue couplings within 6$\mathring{A}$ reproduce residue-wise and pairwise microstate statistics, including correlations between residues that are not directly coupled in the model. Moreover, independently fitted inactive and active reference Hamiltonians define an endpoint preference coordinate that organizes newly sampled ligand-, effector- and conformation-dependent ensembles along the A2A activation landscape without receiving these biochemical labels as model inputs. Finally, a cluster-conditioned all-atom reconstruction model preserves the prescribed residue microstate patterns of newly sampled configurations, closing the coarse-graining-sampling-backmapping cycle. The resulting discrete representation additionally admits direct QUBO encoding, enabling classical annealing and providing a route toward future quantum-annealing implementations. PHASE therefore provides a protein-general procedure for constructing compact, interpretable and atomistically realizable statistical models of protein conformational ensembles.

AI.tldr: PHASE (Protein Hamiltonians for Sampling of Ensembles) converts atomistic conformational ensembles into explicit, interpretable statistical models using local residue couplings. Applied to A2A receptor ensembles from ~37μs of simulations, it reproduces microstate statistics, organizes ensembles along the activation landscape, and enables all-atom reconstruction via cluster conditioning, with a discrete representation suitable for quantum annealing.
AI.motivation: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles represented as high-dimensional probability distributions, yet these distributions are typically only implicit—embedded in simulation trajectories or generative models. There is a need for an explicit and interpretable statistical framework that captures the organization of conformational ensembles.
AI.method: PHASE constructs system-specific Hamiltonians containing only local residue couplings within 6Å to model atomistic conformational ensembles. It fits independent inactive and active reference Hamiltonians to define an endpoint preference coordinate, and uses a cluster-conditioned all-atom reconstruction model to preserve residue microstate patterns. The discrete representation enables direct QUBO encoding for classical and potential quantum annealing.
AI.result: Hamiltonians with only local residue couplings reproduce residue-wise and pairwise microstate statistics, including correlations between residues not directly coupled in the model. The endpoint preference coordinate organizes newly sampled ligand-, effector-, and conformation-dependent ensembles along the A2A activation landscape without requiring biochemical labels. The reconstruction model preserves prescribed microstate patterns, closing the coarse-graining-sampling-backmapping cycle.
AI.conclusion: PHASE provides a protein-general procedure for constructing compact, interpretable, and atomistically realizable statistical models of protein conformational ensembles, with potential applications in classical and quantum annealing-based sampling.

title: The Informational Model of the Holobiont: Statistical Tests for Selection and Extension to a Theory of Variable Interactions
summary: We review, clarify, and generalize a recently proposed evolutionary information-theoretic model of the holobiont, in which evolutionary change is quantified using Jeffreys divergence and partitioned into contributions from the host, microbial components, and host-microbiome associations. Building on these partitions, we develop statistical tests to identify whether observed informational change is attributable to selection acting on host types, microbial-component states, or particular host-microbiome combinations. We then extend the framework to multicomponent groups subject to within- and between-group selection and, ultimately, to a general hierarchical formulation that we call the Theory of Variable Interactions (TVI). In this formulation, biological units may contain interacting components and may themselves form higher-level sets, allowing informational change to be partitioned recursively into marginal and association components across an arbitrary number of organizational levels. The framework encompasses previously studied models of the tragedy of the commons and of aggregate and multicomponent holobiont selection, and, as a further specialization, informational models of non-random mating and sexual selection. TVI therefore provides a unified information-theoretic framework for quantifying evolutionary change in both biological entities and their interactions, with local statistical dimensionality preserved across hierarchical levels while higher levels introduce additional relational dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews, clarifies, and generalizes an evolutionary information-theoretic model of the holobiont, developing statistical tests based on Jeffreys divergence to identify sources of selection. It extends the framework to multicomponent groups and proposes the Theory of Variable Interactions (TVI), a general hierarchical formulation that recursively partitions informational change into marginal and association components across arbitrary organizational levels, unifying models of holobiont selection, tragedy of the commons, and sexual selection.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified information-theoretic framework for quantifying evolutionary change in biological entities and their interactions, generalizing previous holobiont selection models to arbitrary hierarchical organizational levels and encompassing diverse evolutionary phenomena.
AI.method: The framework uses Jeffreys divergence to quantify evolutionary change and partitions it into contributions from hosts, microbial components, and host-microbiome associations. Statistical tests are developed to attribute informational change to selection on host types, microbial-component states, or host-microbiome combinations. The model is extended to multicomponent groups with within/between-group selection and generalized into the recursive hierarchical Theory of Variable Interactions (TVI), which partitions information across arbitrary levels of organization.
AI.result: The framework encompasses previously studied models including tragedy of the commons, aggregate and multicomponent holobiont selection, and informational models of non-random mating and sexual selection, providing a unified information-theoretic approach where local statistical dimensionality is preserved across hierarchical levels while higher levels introduce additional relational dimensions.
AI.conclusion: TVI provides a unified information-theoretic framework for quantifying evolutionary change in biological entities and their interactions, with local statistical dimensionality preserved across hierarchical levels while higher levels introduce additional relational dimensions.

title: HiFiC-G: Adapting HiFiC for Hi-C Contact Matrices
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Bachelor's thesis project, Transilvania University of Brasov (UNITBV). Language editing and translation assistance provided using Claude (Anthropic)
summary: We study whether the loss design of High-Fidelity Generative Image Compression (HiFiC), a GAN-based neural codec originally built for natural photographs, can be adapted to preserve biologically meaningful structure in Hi-C chromatin contact maps under lossy compression. Standard image compression, including HiFiC in its original form, optimizes for human visual perception; but a Hi-C contact map is normally distributed together with its numeric matrix file (.cool/.mcool), which downstream genomic analysis tools consume directly. Aggressive compression that looks acceptable to the eye can nonetheless blur or delete loops and topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries that these tools depend on. We modify HiFiC's distortion term with a spatially-weighted MSE that up-weights biologically salient regions (loops, TAD boundaries, stripes, compartment structure) and add an insulation-score loss term that directly penalizes loss of TAD boundary sharpness. We describe a three-phase fine-tuning strategy that adapts a pretrained HiFiC checkpoint to the Hi-C domain without catastrophic forgetting. We evaluate the resulting system, HiFiC-G, using both conventional image-quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM) and genomics-domain preservation metrics (loop/TAD/compartment/stripe preservation percentage) across two cell lines. HiFiC-G preserves local structure, meaning stripes and TAD boundaries, substantially better than the metrics alone would suggest, while long-range A/B compartment structure remains poorly preserved; we show this gap tracks genomic scale and is consistent with a specific architectural cause, the fixed-size tiling that both HiFiC-G and the original HiFiC rely on for memory efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts HiFiC, a GAN-based neural image codec designed for natural photographs, to compress Hi-C chromatin contact maps while preserving biologically meaningful genomic structure. The authors modify the loss function with spatially-weighted MSE and insulation-score loss, and use a three-phase fine-tuning strategy to create HiFiC-G. Results show good preservation of local structures like loops, stripes, and TAD boundaries, but poor preservation of long-range A/B compartment structure, which they attribute to the fixed-size tiling architecture.
AI.motivation: Hi-C contact maps are shared as numeric matrix files consumed directly by downstream genomic analysis tools, but standard compression optimized for human visual perception can destroy biologically important structures like loops and TAD boundaries even when looking acceptable to the eye.
AI.method: Modifies HiFiC's distortion term with a spatially-weighted MSE that up-weights biologically salient regions (loops, TAD boundaries, stripes, compartments) and adds an insulation-score loss term penalizing loss of TAD boundary sharpness, followed by a three-phase fine-tuning strategy to adapt a pretrained HiFiC checkpoint to the Hi-C domain without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.result: HiFiC-G preserves local structures (stripes, TAD boundaries) substantially better than conventional metrics suggest, but long-range A/B compartment structure remains poorly preserved; this gap tracks genomic scale and is attributed to the fixed-size tiling architecture shared with the original HiFiC.
AI.conclusion: The loss design of a perceptual neural codec can be successfully adapted for genomics-domain preservation in Hi-C compression, though architectural constraints (fixed-size tiling) limit preservation of long-range structures, pointing to a specific design improvement needed for future work.

title: ARCHER: Amortized cross-specimen pose estimation for cryo-electron microscopy
summary: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) pose estimation is traditionally solved anew for each dataset, where iterative refinement is done from scratch while the estimator learns to store the molecule in its weights. In this work, we show that pose inference is a generalizable, specimen-agnostic operation when conditioned explicitly on a reference volume. We introduce ARCHER, an amortized contrastive classifier that models the pose posterior over a discrete rotation grid. Trained across a variety of protein structures, it operates zero-shot without retraining per structure. This transferability is grounded in Fourier-space information mechanics, where all specimen dependence is captured by the reference structure's power spectrum and spatial extent. ARCHER achieves a median angular error of 5.0° on 100 held-out test structures and 2.5° on experimental particles, matching dedicated estimators within 0.16 Å in 3D reconstruction. Crucially, downstream conformational signal is preserved. The leading conformational coordinate correlates at 0.97 with deposited benchmarks, faithfully reconstructing free-energy basins and mobile domains. These results overall demonstrate that cryo-EM pose estimation can be generalized across different structures.

AI.tldr: ARCHER is an amortized contrastive classifier for cryo-EM pose estimation that generalizes zero-shot across protein structures by conditioning on a reference volume, achieving median angular errors of 5.0° on held-out structures and 2.5° on experimental particles while preserving conformational signal.
AI.motivation: Traditional cryo-EM pose estimation is solved from scratch for each new dataset, requiring iterative refinement and storage of molecule-specific parameters, which is computationally expensive and lacks generalizability across specimens.
AI.method: ARCHER is an amortized contrastive classifier that models the pose posterior over a discrete rotation grid, trained across diverse protein structures. It conditions explicitly on a reference volume, leveraging Fourier-space information mechanics where specimen dependence is encoded in the reference structure's power spectrum and spatial extent, enabling zero-shot operation without per-structure retraining.
AI.result: ARCHER achieves 5.0° median angular error on 100 held-out test structures and 2.5° on experimental particles, matching dedicated estimators within 0.16 Å in 3D reconstruction. The leading conformational coordinate correlates at 0.97 with deposited benchmarks, faithfully reconstructing free-energy basins and mobile domains.
AI.conclusion: Cryo-EM pose estimation can be generalized across different structures, demonstrating that specimen-agnostic, amortized pose inference is feasible and preserves downstream conformational analysis quality.

title: Pretreatment DCE-MRI Resolves Response Quality Within Pathologic Endpoints in Neoadjuvant Breast Cancer
summary: Pathologic complete response (pCR) is a strong neoadjuvant endpoint, yet 5-15% of complete responders recur and clinical/genomic variables do not reliably identify them. We tested whether pretreatment dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI entropy - intratumoral enhancement heterogeneity - resolves response quality hidden within pCR and residual cancer burden (RCB). Across four cohorts (1,200 patients), a prespecified entropy threshold defined favorable and adverse structural states. Crossing structure with pathology yielded a four-tier framework spanning 4.1-fold recurrence in I-SPY1 and 7.7-fold at response extremes.
